logline: TVF's Mishra-family dramedy mines the small heartbreaks and warmth of middle-class small-town India, narrated by the family's piggy bank.

renewal.note: TVF's flagship dramedy continues; Season 5 dropped June 2026 with Anant V Joshi recast as Annu. No formal Season 6 confirmation yet.

bollymeter.basis: Comfort-food warmth and lived-in performances hold, even as the writing stretches thinner across seven episodes and absorbs a lead recast.

pull_quotes.text: Great storytelling doesn't need high stakes or shocking twists; the emotional moments continue to resonate.
Once-charming middle-class drama starts to feel stale, the seven-episode season stretched thin.

seasons.review_body: The Mishra house still sounds like home, and that is most of Gullak's job done. Season 5's strength is what it always was: small domestic stakes played with actors who feel like one family. The cost shows in two places the room keeps flagging, a seven-episode run that pads what used to be tight, and a recast Annu that takes adjusting to. Critics split cleanly: the warmth camp scored it generously, the fatigue camp called it comfort food going cold. The audience number stayed high, which for a fifth season is its own verdict on how much goodwill this family has banked.
seasons.season_over_season: Holds the franchise's audience affection but is the first season where multiple critics flagged staleness rather than charm; the recast and longer runtime are the structural shifts from Seasons 1-4.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Mishras are back with a new domestic crisis that feels immediately recognisable. Season 5 opens on the same warmth that made the franchise; the recast Annu is the elephant in the room but the episode has the good sense not to draw attention to it.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Santosh Mishra's first scene at the breakfast table - the show confirming the family still sounds like itself.

critic_note.text: Great storytelling doesn't need high stakes or shocking twists; the emotional moments continue to resonate.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 3
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A family argument about money escalates into something much older and harder to name. The writing here is Gullak doing what it does at its best - locating the grief and love inside a row about the electricity bill.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Shanti's quiet exit from a room that has stopped listening to her - the episode's emotional centre.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 5
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A neighbourhood event pulls the family into the kind of mild social comedy the show handles better than anyone. The longer runtime (seven episodes) is most visible here; what might have been a tight twenty-five minutes runs to forty and feels the difference.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Aman and Annu's argument that lands as reconciliation - the season's warmest beat in its least essential episode.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 7
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 5 finale pulls the family together around a single tender crisis and earns its resolution. The franchise's comfort-food appeal is intact here even where critics noted the overall run had overstayed its welcome.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final piggy-bank narration - the show's oldest trick and, this season, its most honest.

critic_note.text: Once-charming middle-class drama starts to feel stale, the seven-episode season stretched thin.
